1. # Poutine League
2. 
3. ## Vision
4. 
5. Poutine League is an internal, gamified experience that turns the Montreal-based company's shared love of poutine into a fun, social discovery game. Employees submit the best poutines they've found in Montreal restaurants, colleagues try them and leave ratings/reviews, and the community crowns seasonal and all-time champions across several categories — rewarding good taste and generosity in sharing it, not spam-submitting.
6. 
7. The product serves two equally important goals:
8. - **Social bonding** — give colleagues a fun, low-stakes reason to connect, explore the city together, and talk about something other than work.
9. - **AI-native showcase** — serve as a playful, real showcase of what an AI-native Power Platform product can look and feel like, with agentic AI features woven into the core experience rather than bolted on.
10. 
11. This document describes the **functional vision only**. Technical architecture, data model, and implementation choices are intentionally out of scope here.
12. 
13. ## Audience
14. 
15. - Available to **all employees** of the company (Montreal-based only, so no regional restriction needed).
16. - All participants act under their **real employee identity** — submissions, reviews, and leaderboard placements are fully attributed (no anonymity or handles).
17. 
18. ## Core Concepts
19. 
20. ### Submitting a poutine
21. 
22. - Any employee can submit a poutine they believe is one of the best in Montreal.
23. - A submission captures: restaurant/place name and address, poutine name/description, price, a photo, and descriptive **tags** (e.g. classic, smoked meat, vegan, spicy).
24. - Each employee has a **hard cap of 5 active submissions** (configurable in the future). The cap reinforces the "quality over quantity" philosophy: the game rewards showing restraint and proposing only truly excellent poutines, not flooding the list.
25. - New submissions go through **lightweight moderation** before becoming publicly visible. The intent is for an **AI agent to handle first-pass review** (e.g. checking completeness, obvious duplicates, inappropriate content), escalating edge cases to a small group of human moderators/admins.
26. - Before a submission is accepted, an **AI-assisted duplicate/similarity check** runs against existing entries (same restaurant and/or very similar poutine) to avoid redundant or conflicting entries, surfaced directly in the submission flow.
27. 
28. ### Trying and reviewing a poutine
29. 
30. - "Trying" a poutine is **self-declared** (honor system): an employee marks a poutine as tried, then rates and reviews it. No photo or check-in proof is required.
31. - A review consists of a **star rating (1–5)** plus a **short written comment**.
32. - Reviews and ratings are visible to everyone, tied to the reviewer's real name.
33. 
34. ### Discovery
35. 
36. - Employees can browse and discover poutines through both:
37.   - A **list/feed view** with filtering by tags, neighborhood, rating, etc.
38.   - A **map view** centered on Montreal showing where each submitted poutine can be found.
39. 
40. ## Gamification: Categories & Leaderboards
41. 
42. Two parallel timeframes are tracked:
43. - An **all-time Hall of Fame**, continuously updated.
44. - **Seasonal contests**, aligned with the four seasons (winter, spring, summer, autumn) — since poutine recommendations naturally shift with the seasons. Each season resets and crowns a **single winner (top 1)** per category.
45. 
46. Launch categories:
47. 
48. 1. **Best Seller** — the employee whose submitted poutine(s) got the most colleagues to try them. Recognizes people who are good at "selling" their picks to others.
49. 2. **Top Poutine** — the highest-rated poutine for the period. To be fair to poutines with few votes, this uses a **confidence-weighted rating** (a dynamic average that accounts for both the average score and the number of reviews, similar in spirit to a Bayesian/weighted average) so that a poutine with a very high rating but very few reviews doesn't automatically outrank one with a strong rating backed by many reviews. Borderline cases should be flagged for review rather than resolved purely automatically.
50. 3. **Best Supporter** — the employee who tried the most poutines. The "poutine lover"/most supportive taste-tester of the community.
51. 4. **Best Critic** — the employee whose written reviews are considered the most helpful/insightful (exact evaluation approach to be refined, potentially AI-assisted).
52. 
53. Notes:
54. - Submitters are explicitly **not** rewarded for volume — the submission cap and the category design both discourage spamming and instead reward selectivity, popularity, quality, and engagement.
55. - Winner rewards (badges/titles vs. tangible prizes) are **not yet decided** and are left open for a future decision — the experience should work purely on symbolic recognition (badges, titles, leaderboard bragging rights, Hall of Fame entries) at minimum.
56. - Additional categories may be introduced over time (the list above is the launch set, not final).
57. 
58. ## Agentic AI Features
59. 
60. Agentic AI is meant to be infused throughout the experience rather than as a single add-on feature. Priorities for a first version:
61. 
62. 1. **Duplicate/similarity detection during submission** — proactively flags likely-duplicate restaurants or poutines as someone is submitting, before it reaches moderation.
63. 2. **AI-assisted moderation** — an agent performs first-pass review of new submissions (completeness, obvious issues, duplicate signals) and escalates ambiguous cases to human moderators/admins instead of blocking or approving blindly.
64. 3. **Fun facts / trivia generation** — the agent surfaces fun, engaging trivia or context about a submitted poutine or restaurant (e.g. history, ingredients, fun comparisons) to reinforce the playful, gamified feel.
65. 4. **Conversational assistant** — a chat-style agent employees can talk to for help using the product and getting recommendations (e.g. "what's the best vegan poutine downtown?", "help me find a poutine I haven't tried yet").
66. 
67. Other AI ideas discussed but not prioritized for launch (candidates for later iterations): personalized recommendations based on taste history, AI-generated review summaries/sentiment digests per poutine.
68. 
69. ## Notifications
70. 
71. Kept intentionally minimal at launch to avoid noise: employees are notified primarily about **season results and category winner announcements**. Day-to-day activity (someone trying your poutine, new reviews, etc.) is discovered by employees browsing the app rather than through push notifications. This can be revisited later if engagement needs a boost.
72. 
73. ## Out of Scope (for this document)
74. 
75. - Technical architecture, data model, integrations, and hosting decisions.
76. - Final decision on winner rewards (symbolic-only vs. tangible prizes).
77. - Final list of all gamification categories beyond the launch set.
78. - Detailed moderation team composition and escalation process.
79.

1. # Poutine League — Architecture
2. 
3. This document describes the initial **Power Platform-centric technical architecture** for Poutine League, derived from the functional vision in [`PRODUCT.md`](./PRODUCT.md). It captures decisions made so far and flags open questions to resolve during implementation.
4. 
5. The architecture leans **exclusively** on four Power Platform building blocks:
6. 
7. | Building block | Role in this product |
8. |---|---|
9. | **Dataverse** | System of record for the data model, plus the mechanism for injecting sample/demo data. |
10. | **Power Automate cloud flows** | Non-AI, deterministic backend processes (scheduling, aggregation, notifications, geocoding). |
11. | **Power Apps code apps** | Front-end experiences (employee app + admin app). |
12. | **Copilot Studio agents (GitHub Copilot harness)** | AI agentic experiences — one interactive conversational agent, and specialized headless agents for backend AI reasoning. |
13. 
14. > [!NOTE]
15. > This document favors a **single Dev environment with one unmanaged solution** for the demo. Multi-environment promotion is intentionally out of scope for the live demo (see [ALM & environments](#alm--environments)), even though a deterministic CD pipeline already exists in this repo as a forward-looking illustration.
16. 
17. ## 1. Data model (Dataverse)
18. 
19. Dataverse is the single system of record. All entities below are custom tables unless noted otherwise.
20. 
21. | Table | Purpose | Key fields (indicative) |
22. |---|---|---|
23. | **Restaurant** | A Montreal restaurant/place where a poutine was found. | Name, address, geocoded latitude/longitude, city area/neighborhood. |
24. | **Poutine Submission** | A submitted poutine, owned by the submitting employee. | Name/description, price, photo (Dataverse file/image column), tags, status (`Draft` → `Submitted` → `In Review` → `Approved`/`Rejected`), lookup to Restaurant, lookup to submitter (system user). |
25. | **Tag** | Descriptive tag (classic, smoked meat, vegan, spicy, …). | Name. Many-to-many with Poutine Submission. |
26. | **Try** | An employee self-declaring they tried a poutine. | Lookup to Poutine Submission, lookup to employee (system user), timestamp. |
27. | **Review** | Rating + comment left after a Try. | Star rating (1–5), comment text, lookup to Try/Poutine Submission, lookup to reviewer (system user), AI-assessed helpfulness score (nullable, populated by the review-scoring backend agent). |
28. | **Season** | A seasonal contest period (winter/spring/summer/autumn). | Start/end date, status (`Active`/`Closed`). |
29. | **Category** | A leaderboard category (Best Seller, Top Poutine, Best Supporter, Best Critic, + future ones). | Name, description, computation type. |
30. | **Season Result** | Persisted, nightly-computed leaderboard standing per season/category. | Lookup to Season, lookup to Category, ranked entries (employee or poutine + score), computed-at timestamp. |
31. | **Hall of Fame Entry** | All-time winners, archived at season close. | Lookup to Season, lookup to Category, winner (employee or poutine), badge/title text. |
32. 
33. **Employees are Dataverse system users backed by Entra ID** — no custom Employee table. Submissions, tries, and reviews are attributed via lookups to `systemuser`, keeping identity/auth outside the app's data model.
34.

130. > [!NOTE]

132. 
133. ### Security roles
134. 
135. - **Admin/Moderator**: a small group (2–3 people) using the built-in **System Administrator** security role — acceptable at this scale/org, keeps setup simple, no custom role needed.
136. - **Employee**: follows the **principle of least privilege** — read access to all public data (submissions, reviews, leaderboards), write access scoped to their own submissions/tries/reviews only. Exact field- and record-level privileges to be defined as a custom security role when building the code apps.
137. 
138. ### Confirmed decisions
139. 
140. - **Restaurant stays normalized as its own table** (as modeled above) — gives a cleaner data model, clear separation of concerns per table, and enables future capabilities like tracking which restaurants keep appearing across seasons.
141. - **`Season Result` stores a full ranked-list snapshot per season/category**, not just the top-1 winner — even though only the top-1 is announced/crowned at season close, the fuller snapshot supports richer leaderboard history and analytics later.
142. 
143. ## 2. AI agentic experiences (Copilot Studio, GitHub Copilot harness)
144. 
145. All Copilot Studio agents in this product are built on the **[GitHub Copilot harness](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/harnesses-overview)** (no classic "topics" — reasoning-driven, tool/knowledge/connected-agent orchestration).
146. 
147. ### 2.1 Interactive conversational agent (single entry point)
148. 
149. One agent serves as the **single conversational entry point** for employees — submitting/managing poutines, exploring poutines to try, and checking the leaderboard, all through natural-language interaction. It is:
150. 
151. - **Embedded inside the employee-facing code app** (chat panel), and
152. - **Also published standalone to Microsoft 365 Copilot**,
153. 
154. so employees can reach it from either surface. It uses Dataverse as a tool/knowledge source to read and write submissions, tries, and reviews on the user's behalf, respecting the same security roles as the code app.
155. 
156. ### 2.2 Specialized backend agents (headless, non-interactive)
157. 
158. Backend AI reasoning is split into **specialized agents**, each with a narrow responsibility, invoked as backend processes rather than through chat:
159. 
160. | Backend agent | Responsibility | Triggered by |
161. |---|---|---|
162. | **Submission Review agent** | Combines completeness check, duplicate/similarity detection (same restaurant/very similar poutine), and first-pass moderation; escalates ambiguous cases instead of deciding blindly. | Poutine Submission status change `Draft` → `Submitted` (see [submission flow](#3-submission-review-flow)). |
163. | **Fun Facts agent** | Generates engaging trivia/context about an approved poutine or restaurant, grounded in Dataverse data (submission details, tags, restaurant info) and the model's general knowledge — **no external web search grounding**, to keep the demo self-contained. | Poutine Submission reaching `Approved` status; may also be reused on-demand as a connected-agent tool by the interactive agent when an employee asks for a fun fact in chat. |
164. | **Review Quality agent** | Scores review helpfulness/insightfulness to power the "Best Critic" category. | Nightly leaderboard computation flow (§4). |
165. 
166. > [!NOTE]
167. > **Multi-agent design follows Microsoft's guidance**: keep it to one interactive agent as the default entry point, and only split into specialized agents where there's a distinct domain, distinct trigger, or reusability need — which is the case for review, fun facts, and review-quality scoring.
168. 
169. ## 3. Submission review flow
170. 
171. 1. An employee starts a **Poutine Submission** in `Draft` status via the employee code app (or the conversational agent).
172. 2. When ready, they move it to `Submitted`.
173. 3. The **Submission Review agent** is invoked from a **Power Automate cloud flow** triggered on that Dataverse status change, and performs completeness + duplicate/similarity + first-pass moderation checks.
174. 4. Clear-cut outcomes move the record straight to `Approved` or `Rejected`.
175. 5. Ambiguous cases are flagged `In Review` and escalated to a human moderator/admin.
176. 
177. ### Escalation mechanism (open question — see below)
178. 
179. - **Primary (aspirational)**: use Copilot Studio's **[Request for Information (RFI)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot/blog/copilot-studio/introducing-request-for-information-in-copilot-studio-agent-flows/)** human-in-the-loop node inside a **Copilot Studio Workflow**, emailing the moderator a structured form and feeding the response back into the flow.
180. - **Fallback (primary for the demo)**: flag the Dataverse record `In Review`, surface it in the **admin code app**'s review queue, and send a lightweight **Microsoft Teams heads-up notification** via Power Automate.
181. 
182. > [!IMPORTANT]
183. > Copilot Studio **Workflows** are not yet supported by the Copilot Studio-related skills/plugins used in this repo (`skills-for-copilot-studio`, `copilot-studio-plugin`). Until that changes, **Power Automate cloud flows call specialized Copilot Studio agents directly** via the **[Microsoft Copilot Studio connector](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/connectors/microsoftcopilotstudio/)** as the one consistent AI-invocation pattern across the product. Adopting Copilot Studio Workflows (and the RFI node) for the submission-review escalation is a **future exploration to keep an eye on** as Microsoft's tooling evolves — it is not expected to land in time for this demo.
184. 
185. ## 4. Non-AI backend processes (Power Automate cloud flows)
186. 
187. | Flow | Purpose | Trigger |
188. |---|---|---|
189. | **Submission review orchestration** | Calls the Submission Review agent (**[Execute Agent and wait](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/connectors/microsoftcopilotstudio/#execute-agent-and-wait)** — needs the agent's decision synchronously to apply it to the record) and applies its outcome to the Dataverse record. | Dataverse: Poutine Submission status → `Submitted`. |
190. | **Geocoding** | Resolves a submitted restaurant address to latitude/longitude for the map view, using the free tier of [geocod.io](https://www.geocod.io/free-geocoding). | Dataverse: new/updated Restaurant address. |
191. | **Fun facts generation** | Calls the Fun Facts agent (**[Execute Agent and wait](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/connectors/microsoftcopilotstudio/#execute-agent-and-wait)**) and stores the result once a submission is approved. | Dataverse: Poutine Submission status → `Approved`. |
192. | **Nightly leaderboard computation** | Recomputes and persists standings for all live categories (including calling the Review Quality agent — **[Execute Agent and wait](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/connectors/microsoftcopilotstudio/#execute-agent-and-wait)** — for Best Critic) into `Season Result`. | Scheduled (nightly). |
193. | **Season rollover** | Closes the active season, crowns the top-1 winner per category, archives to `Hall of Fame Entry`, opens the next season. | Scheduled (quarterly/date-based, aligned to season boundaries). |
194. | **Winner announcement notification** | Notifies employees of season results and category winners. | Triggered by the season rollover flow; delivered via **Microsoft Teams**. |
195. 
196. Live leaderboard views inside the code apps are **computed on demand by the code app** from raw Dataverse data (ratings, tries, reviews) for responsiveness; the nightly flow's persisted `Season Result` snapshot is the durable, "official" record used for history, badges, and season-close/Hall of Fame purposes.
197. 
198. > [!NOTE]
199. > All flow → agent calls use the **[Microsoft Copilot Studio connector](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/connectors/microsoftcopilotstudio/)**. Use **[Execute Agent and wait](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/connectors/microsoftcopilotstudio/#execute-agent-and-wait)** when the flow needs the agent's response synchronously to continue (all cases above); the fire-and-forget **[Execute Agent](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/connectors/microsoftcopilotstudio/#execute-agent)** action remains available for any future scenario that doesn't need to block on a response.
200. 
201. ## 5. Front-end experiences (Power Apps code apps)
202. 
203. Two separate code apps, both connecting to Dataverse:
204. 
205. 1. **Employee app** — submit/manage poutines (respecting the 5 active-submission cap), browse/discover (list + map views, using an open-source JS map library such as Leaflet with geocoded coordinates from Dataverse), mark poutines as tried, leave reviews, view leaderboards and Hall of Fame, and access the embedded conversational agent.
206. 2. **Admin/moderation app** — review queue for escalated submissions, override approve/reject decisions, manage categories/seasons, and any other admin utilities.
207. 
208. ## 6. Sample/demo data
209. 
210. Dataverse also serves as the target for **sample data injection** used for testing and demos: seed data (restaurants, poutines, tags, reviews, seasons) is authored as CSV/JSON files in the repo and loaded via the **Dataverse skill's bulk/data import capability**, keeping seeding reproducible and reviewable in source control rather than a one-off script or flow.
211. 
212. ## 7. ALM & environments
213. 
214. - **Primary focus for this architecture and the live demo: a single Dev environment with one unmanaged solution.** All components (tables, flows, code apps, agents) live in this one solution during active development.
215. - The repo already includes a forward-looking, deterministic CD pipeline (`.github/workflows/deploy-solution.yml`) that packs and imports changed solutions to a target environment via PAC CLI + OIDC on merges to `main`. It's meant to **illustrate** the target promotion pattern — keeping deployment deterministic and human-reviewed through PRs — rather than to be exercised live during the demo.
216. - Multi-environment promotion (Dev → Test/Prod), managed vs. unmanaged solution strategy at scale, and connection reference/environment variable management across environments are **explicitly deferred** — see the `solution-management` skill for the mechanics when this becomes relevant.
217.

275. 
276. - [ ] Whether/when to adopt Copilot Studio **Workflows** + the **Request for Information** node for submission-review escalation — keep an eye on Microsoft's roadmap, but not expected to be ready in time for this demo. Current fallback is Dataverse flag + admin app queue + Teams notification.

1. # mcdm26-ai-native-powerplatform-dev
2. 
3. Demo companion repository for [**AI-Native Power Platform Development: Building from the IDE**, prepared for **Microsoft Community Days Montreal 2026**](https://www.communitydays.org/event/2026-08-21/microsoft-community-days-montreal#sessions?id=1236475).
4. 
5. This repository is the working space for presentation-aligned demonstrations that show how Power Platform work can move from a browser-first experience to an **AI-native, IDE-centered workflow**. The goal is not to prove that one tool replaces every other tool. The goal is to show where AI-assisted development fits, where review gates still matter, and how to structure the work so the results stay reliable.
6. 
7. > [!NOTE]
8. > This is an early bootstrap repository. The structure is intentionally generic for now, and concrete demo assets will be added incrementally as the session build-out progresses.
9. 
10. ## Session framing
11. 
12. Most attendees already know the traditional Power Platform maker experience in the browser. This repo supports a session that explores:
13. 
14. - why teams may want an IDE-centered workflow
15. - what tradeoffs come with that shift
16. - where AI agents help across the delivery lifecycle
17. - which review, approval, and ALM gates should remain human-controlled
18. 
19. ## Technology areas being explored
20. 
21. The current working stack includes:
22. 
23. - [**GitHub Copilot App**](https://github.com/features/ai/github-app) and [**GitHub Copilot**](https://github.com/features/copilot)
24. - [**microsoft/power-platform-skills**](https://github.com/microsoft/power-platform-skills)
25. - [**microsoft/Dataverse-skills**](https://github.com/microsoft/Dataverse-skills)
26. - [**microsoft/skills-for-copilot-studio**](https://github.com/microsoft/skills-for-copilot-studio) and [**microsoft/copilot-studio-plugin**](https://github.com/microsoft/copilot-studio-plugin)
27. - [**Entire**](https://entire.io/)
28. - [**GitHub stacked PRs**](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-30-stacked-pull-requests-are-now-in-public-preview/)
29. 
30. > [!NOTE]

39. Break any non-trivial change into a stack of small, independently-reviewable PRs using `gh-stack`. Each layer is its own nested session and worktree, spawned from a coordinator session.

41. ### Entire traceability protocol (mandatory)
42. 
43. Use this exact flow for every branch/worktree in this repo:
44. 
45. ```powershell
46. # 1. Capture observability evidence before finalization
47. Set-Location <path-to-nested-worktree>
48. make entire-observe
49. 
50. # 2. Run dry attach decision first (never skip)
51. make entire-link-dry
52. 
53. # 3. Apply only when dry output is acceptable
54. make entire-link-apply

56. # 4. If apply is blocked but branch must be recovered, use explicit runtime session ID
57. #    (from ~/.copilot/session-state/<project-session-id>/workspace.yaml or events.jsonl)
58. make entire-link-apply-unsafe SESSION_ID=<runtime-session-id>
59. 
60. # 5. Finalize and verify branch-head trailer posture
61. make entire-stack-finalize
62. 
63. # 6. Push branch state
64. git push origin <branch-name> --force-with-lease
65. ```
66. 
67. > [!WARNING]
68. > **Do not run raw `entire session attach ... --force` by default.** Use helper targets first. Raw attach is break-glass only when helper flow cannot proceed.
69. 
70. > [!WARNING]
71. > **Single-writer rule (mandatory):** never run overlapping attach operations from multiple sessions on the same branch/worktree. We reproduced silent trailer replacement (`Entire-Checkpoint`) under concurrent raw attaches.
72. 
73. > [!TIP]
74. > If `entire session current` resolves to an ended/wrong session, resolve runtime session ID from `~/.copilot/session-state/<project-session-id>/workspace.yaml` and use `SESSION_ID=...` explicit mode.
75. 
76. > [!NOTE]
77. > Do not modify `.github/hooks/entire.json` — it is managed by `entire agent add` and overwritten on reinstall.
78. 
79. > [!NOTE]
80. > In autopilot worktrees, `workspace.yaml` can keep the creation-time branch name after `rename_branch`; treat branch mismatch as expected drift and resolve by git root + recency.
81. 
82. ### Troubleshooting: entire activity shows too few sessions
83. 
84. `entire activity` only reflects checkpoints linked to current branch heads. In stacked workflows, rebases and force-pushes can drop trailer coverage from some layers. Use this checklist to diagnose and recover.
85. 
86. **1. Check trailer presence per branch**
87. 
88. ```powershell
89. # Run from repo root — replace branch names with your stack
90. foreach($b in @(
91.   'rpothin-add-orchestrator-skills',
92.   'rpothin-feat-makefile-and-deployment-workflow',
93.   'rpothin-init-agents-md',
94.   'rpothin-add-gitignore-hardening'
95. )){
96.   git --no-pager log -1 --format='%H %s' origin/$b
97.   $msg = git --no-pager log -1 --format=%B origin/$b
98.   if($msg -match 'Entire-Checkpoint:'){ ($msg | Select-String 'Entire-Checkpoint:').Line } else { 'NO_TRAILER' }
99.   ''
100. }
101. ```
102. 
103. Any branch printing `NO_TRAILER` is not currently linked at HEAD and will be missing from `entire activity`.
104. 
105. **2. Recover a branch**
106. 
107. ```powershell
108. Set-Location <layer-worktree>
109. make entire-link-apply-unsafe SESSION_ID=<runtime-session-id>
110. make entire-stack-finalize
111. git push origin <branch> --force-with-lease   # if not already pushed by helper flow
112. ```
113. 
114. > [!WARNING]
115. > Any commit after attach/finalize can invalidate branch-head traceability. Re-run the mandatory protocol before merge.
116. 
117. **3. Reliable finalization protocol for stacked sessions**
118. 
119. 1. Keep lower layers stable while reviewing upper layers.
120. 2. Do all development and rebases first.
121. 3. When a layer is finalised, run the **mandatory helper protocol** (`entire-observe` -> `entire-link-dry` -> `entire-link-apply`/`entire-link-apply-unsafe` -> `entire-stack-finalize`) as the **last step**.
122. 4. If you commit again on that layer, re-run the mandatory helper protocol.
123. 5. Before merge, run a final bottom→top mandatory helper pass across all open stack branches, then make no further commits.
124. 
125. Persistent under-count in `entire activity` after syncing usually means one or more branch heads have `NO_TRAILER`.

127. **Prerequisite — `commit_linking: always`:** `.entire/settings.json` must contain `"commit_linking": "always"`. Without it, the interactive linking prompt is silently declined in non-interactive agent subprocess commits. This is already set in the repo; if Entire is re-initialized, restore this setting before making any commits. Note: this setting only helps when the session is genuinely active (live `sessionStart`). In Copilot App nested sessions, session state can still resolve to `ended`; use the mandatory helper protocol with explicit runtime `SESSION_ID` recovery mode when needed.

98. # Design System: Poutine League
99. 
100. ## Overview
101. 
102. **Creative North Star: "The Comptoir Championship"**
103. 
104. Poutine League looks like the laminated menu board and hand-painted sign above a beloved Montreal casse-croûte — warm, confident, a little cheeky, built to be read at a glance from the counter. The system takes its cues from comptoir culture: chalkboard specials, sticker-badged loyalty cards, laminated table numbers, and the taped-up "Champion of the Month" photo by the register. It exists to make an internal work tool feel like a neighborhood ritual, not a dashboard.
105. 
106. Flat and graphic, never soft or glassy: surfaces separate with ink-black outlines and hard offset shadows like laminated cardstock, not blurred drop shadows. Fry-gold is the one color every screen is built around; ketchup-red is reserved and only appears where it means something (a call to action, a live rating, an alert). Rejected explicitly: cold blues/grays, glassmorphism, soft blurred shadows, gradient mesh backgrounds, and generic rounded-icon-tile chrome — none of it belongs in a casse-croûte.
107. 
108. The admin/moderation app inherits the same palette, type, and shape language, but its composition is calmer and denser — a back-of-house control panel run by the same counter, not a second brand.
109. 
110. **Key Characteristics:**
111. - Hand-painted sign-board display type paired with a clean workhorse body face for scanability.
112. - One dominant saturated color (fry-gold) per screen; ketchup-red stays rare and meaningful.
113. - Flat surfaces, ink-black borders, hard offset "sticker" shadows — no blur, no glass.
114. - Checkerboard motif used sparingly as a divider/accent, never as a busy full background.
115. - Pill-shaped chips and badges everywhere small facts (tags, ranks, status) need to be scanned fast.
116. 
117. ## Colors
118. 
119. A warm, committed palette: fry-gold carries the surface, ketchup-red is the rare exclamation mark, and everything else sits in creamy counter-neutrals.
120. 
121. ### Primary
122. - **Fry Gold** (`#D99A2B`): the system's dominant color — primary buttons, active nav state, header bands, hero sections, the "one griddle" every screen is built around.
123. - **Fry Gold Deep** (`#B87A1C`): hover/active/pressed state for fry-gold surfaces.
124. 
125. ### Secondary
126. - **Ketchup Red** (`#C23B2E`): reserved for meaning, not decoration — primary CTAs that commit an action (submit, approve), live star ratings, and destructive/alert states.
127. - **Ketchup Red Deep** (`#9C2B21`): hover/active state for ketchup-red surfaces.
128. 
129. ### Tertiary
130. - **Relish Green** (`#5C7A3A`): approved/success states only (submission approved, connection healthy).
131. - **Mustard Amber** (`#E0A419`): pending/in-review states only (submission in moderation, season in progress).
132. 
133. ### Neutral
134. - **Cream Counter** (`#FBF3E6`): page background — the laminate-countertop base, never stark white.
135. - **Paper White** (`#FFFDF8`): card/surface background, one step lighter than the page for gentle separation.
136. - **Checker Light** (`#EDD9B8`): tag chips, table zebra-striping, and the checkerboard accent motif.
137. - **Gravy Ink** (`#2A1D14`): borders and outlines — the "hand-painted line" that separates every surface.
138. - **Gravy Text** (`#3A2A1E`): primary body/heading text color.
139. - **Gravy Text Soft** (`#6B5644`): secondary/meta text (timestamps, helper copy, counts).
140. 
141. ### Named Rules
142. **The One Griddle Rule.** Fry-gold owns exactly one dominant region per screen — a header band, a hero card, or the primary CTA — never more than one at a time. Spend it once per screen or it stops feeling special.
143. 
144. **The Ketchup Is Punctuation Rule.** Ketchup-red never fills a background or a large region. It marks the single thing on a screen that wants a reaction: submit, approve, a 5-star badge, a "your turn" alert.
145. 
146. ## Typography
147. 
148. **Display Font:** Alfa Slab One (with Georgia, serif fallback)
149. **Body Font:** Inter (with system-ui, sans-serif fallback)
150. **Label/Score Font:** ui-monospace stack (SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Consolas)
151. 
152. **Character:** Alfa Slab One brings the thick, confident stroke of a hand-painted menu board to hero moments and section titles; Inter stays out of the way for everything an employee actually has to read and act on. The monospace score face gives ranks, ratings, and prices the tabular precision of a scoreboard.
153. 
154. ### Hierarchy
155. - **Display** (400, `clamp(2.25rem, 5vw, 3.75rem)`, 1.05): page heroes, season-winner announcements, empty-state headlines.
156. - **Headline** (400, `clamp(1.5rem, 3vw, 2.25rem)`, 1.1): section titles ("Leaderboard", "Review Queue"), card group headers.
157. - **Title** (700, 1.25rem, 1.3): card titles (poutine name, restaurant name), button labels.
158. - **Body** (400, 1rem, 1.5): reviews, descriptions, form fields. Wrap at 65–75ch for reviews and comments.
159. - **Label** (600, 0.8125rem, 1.2, 0.02em tracking): tag chips, status badges, table headers — uppercase where used as a category marker.
160. - **Score** (700, 1.125rem, 1, mono, tabular): star ratings, leaderboard ranks, prices, review counts.
161. 
162. ### Named Rules
163. **The Menu Board Rule.** Alfa Slab One is for moments that deserve a beat — hero, headline, a crowned winner. It never appears in body copy, form labels, or dense admin tables; there it steps aside for Inter.
164. 
165. ## Layout
166. 
167. A single comfortable content column (max 1200px) with generous top-of-section spacing over bottom, matching the spacing scale (4/8/16/24/40px). Employee app screens breathe — cards have room, the map/list toggle sits prominently, leaderboards use full-width rank rows. The admin app tightens the same rhythm: denser tables, smaller card padding (use `sm`/`md` spacing over `lg`/`xl`), more rows visible per screen, because its 2–3 users optimize for throughput over atmosphere. Both apps share the same 12px grid baseline and the same breakpoint behavior: single column below 640px, two-column card grids from 640–1024px, full multi-column leaderboard/table layouts above 1024px.
168. 
169. ## Elevation & Depth
170. 
171. Flat by design, with depth conveyed through ink-black outlines and hard, unblurred offset shadows — like laminated cardstock stacked on a counter, never glass or soft ambient light. Nothing in this system uses `blur()`, gradient meshes, or floating glass panels.
172. 
173. ### Shadow Vocabulary
174. - **Sticker** (`box-shadow: 3px 3px 0 #2A1D14`): default resting shadow for cards, buttons, and badges — a hard, single-direction offset with zero blur.
175. - **Sticker Pressed** (`box-shadow: 1px 1px 0 #2A1D14`): active/pressed state, shadow compresses as the element "sits down" on the counter.
176. - **Sticker Lifted** (`box-shadow: 5px 5px 0 #2A1D14`): hover state on interactive cards, shadow grows slightly as if peeling up off the counter.
177. 
178. ### Named Rules
179. **The Laminate Rule.** Depth comes from a hard offset shadow and a visible ink border, never from blur. If a surface needs to look "elevated," give it more offset — not more blur.
180. 
181. ## Shapes
182. 
183. Borders are the load-bearing visual device: every card, button, and chip carries a 2px `gravy-ink` outline, echoing a hand-painted sign's confident line. Corners are generously rounded — `sm` (6px) for tight controls, `md` (12px) for cards, `lg` (20px) for hero/feature cards — evoking laminated menu cards and rounded diner signage rather than sharp corporate rectangles. Interactive chips, badges, and primary/secondary buttons are full pills (`999px`), like loyalty-card stamps or rank medals. The checkerboard motif (alternating `cream-counter`/`checker-light` squares) appears only as a thin divider strip or footer/header band accent — never as a full-page background, where it would overwhelm content.
184. 
185. ## Components
186. 
187. ### Buttons
188. - **Shape:** full pill (`999px` radius), 2px `gravy-ink` border, Sticker shadow at rest.
189. - **Primary:** `fry-gold` background, `gravy-ink` text, Title typography, 12px/28px padding. Reserved for the one primary action per screen (Submit, Approve).
190. - **Secondary:** `paper-white` background, `gravy-ink` text and border, same shape/padding — used for all non-primary actions.
191. - **Destructive/Alert:** same shape, `ketchup-red` background, `paper-white` text — reject, delete, cancel actions only.
192. - **Hover / Focus:** background shifts to the `-deep` variant; shadow grows to Sticker Lifted; focus ring is a 3px `gravy-ink` outline offset 2px, never a soft glow.
193. 
194. ### Chips (tags, status)
195. - **Style:** `checker-light` background, `gravy-text` label type, full pill, no border (chips are quieter than cards/buttons).
196. - **State:** status chips swap fill color by meaning — `mustard-amber` for in-review, `relish-green` for approved, `ketchup-red` for rejected — always paired with a text label, never color alone.
197. 
198. ### Cards / Containers
199. - **Corner Style:** `md` (12px) for poutine/review cards, `lg` (20px) for hero/leaderboard-winner cards.
200. - **Border/Shadow:** 2px `gravy-ink` border + Sticker shadow at rest, Sticker Lifted on hover for anything clickable.
201. - **Content Rhythm:** image/photo first (poutine photo), Title below, meta row (rating score, tag chips) beneath that, using `sm`–`md` internal spacing.
202. 
203. ### Leaderboard / Rank Badges
204. - **Shape:** circular, 40px, `fry-gold` fill, `gravy-ink` border, Score typography centered.
205. - **Top-1 treatment:** the current season/all-time #1 gets a `mustard-amber` ring accent outside the badge border — the closest this system gets to a literal medal, used sparingly (only true #1 placements, never generic "featured" tagging).
206. 
207. ### Map & List Views (Employee app discovery)
208. - **List rows:** card treatment above, one row per poutine, rank/score right-aligned in Score typography.
209. - **Map pins:** circular `fry-gold`-filled pins with `gravy-ink` border matching the rank-badge shape language, so map and list feel like one system, not two.
210. 
211. ## Do's and Don'ts
212. 
213. **Do:**
214. - Spend fry-gold once per screen as the dominant region (header, hero, or primary CTA).
215. - Keep every border `gravy-ink`, every shadow hard-offset with zero blur.
216. - Use the checkerboard motif only as a thin accent strip, never a full background.
217. - Give the admin app the same palette and shapes, just tighter spacing and smaller type scale usage.
218. - Pair every status color with a text label — never rely on color alone for meaning.
219. 
220. **Don't:**
221. - Don't use soft blurred shadows, glassmorphism, or gradient-mesh backgrounds — this system is flat and hard-edged by doctrine.
222. - Don't let ketchup-red fill a background, nav bar, or large region — it's punctuation, not paint.
223. - Don't introduce cool blues/grays or stock "SaaS" gradient icon tiles — everything visual should feel hand-made for a casse-croûte, not a generic dashboard template.
224. - Don't use Alfa Slab One for body copy, table cells, or form labels — reserve it for hero/headline moments only.
225. - Don't stack more than one rounded-radius scale on the same element family (e.g., don't mix `md` and `lg` cards in the same grid).

13. # app-implementation
14. 
15. Orchestration layer for all Power Apps Code App work in this project.
16. The `code-apps-preview` plugin provides the full scaffold-to-deploy lifecycle.

21. `create-code-app`, `add-dataverse`, `add-sharepoint`, `add-excel`, `add-onedrive`,

24. 
25. If any required sub-skill is missing or unavailable:
26. 1. Stop execution and return a blocked status.
27. 2. Ask the user whether they want to install or enable the missing dependency.
28. 3. Resume only after availability is confirmed.
29. 
30. Do not handcraft connector scaffolding or generated bindings as a fallback for missing skills.
31. 
32. ## Step 1 — Environment and solution scope gate (required)
33. 
34. Before any code-app work starts, require explicit target scope:
35. - Environment: display name and environment ID (or URL)
36. - Solution: unique name and publisher prefix for the solution that will contain app assets
37. 
38. If either environment or solution is missing, ambiguous, or inferred:
39. 1. Stop execution and return a blocked status.
40. 2. Ask the user to explicitly provide the target environment and solution.
41. 3. Resume only after both are confirmed.
42. 
43. Do not scaffold, connect data sources, or deploy against an implicit target.
44. 
45. ## Step 2 — Design alignment with Impeccable (strongly recommended)
46. 
47. Power Apps code apps are React apps. Run the `impeccable` skill to establish and maintain
48. design quality throughout the full lifecycle, not just at init.
49. 
50. ### Shared DESIGN.md + per-app PRODUCT.md pattern
51. 
52. This is natively supported by Impeccable's monorepo path resolution:
53. 
54. - **Shared `DESIGN.md`** — lives at `code-apps/DESIGN.md`. One design system, all apps.
55. - **Shared `.impeccable/`** — lives at `code-apps/` with a `config.json` declaring each
56.   `code-apps/<app-name>` as a `projectRoot`. This tells Impeccable to walk up and find the
57.   shared DESIGN.md when running inside any app subfolder.
58. - **Per-app `PRODUCT.md`** — lives at `code-apps/<app-name>/PRODUCT.md`. Product context
59.   (users, purpose, brand personality, constraints) is specific to each app.
60. 
61. **One-time setup (before first code app):** run `impeccable document` at `code-apps/` to
62. generate the shared `DESIGN.md`. This captures the design system that all apps in the project
63. will inherit. If no code exists yet, use `impeccable new-work` to establish the visual world
64. from scratch. Do not scaffold or build any code app before this step.
65. 
66. **Per-app setup (before each new code app):** run `impeccable init --target code-apps/<app-name>/`
67. to write the app's `PRODUCT.md`. This interview pins product context (users, purpose, brand
68. personality, constraints) to the app before any code is written.
69. 
70. Impeccable resolves the shared `DESIGN.md` automatically via the `config.json` `projectRoots`
71. when running inside any app subfolder.
72. 
73. ### Design artifact governance
74. 
75. `DESIGN.md`, `PRODUCT.md`, and `.impeccable/` files are human-owned. Do not write or modify
76. them autonomously during a working session.
77. 
78. When the agent identifies that an update would improve accuracy (e.g., new design tokens
79. introduced, product scope shifted, a component was added):
80. 
81. 1. **Formulate the proposed change**: describe what would change and why.
82. 2. **Present it to the user** and wait for explicit approval.
83. 3. **Apply only if approved**. If declined, note the divergence and continue.
84. 
85. This applies to every write — including minor corrections, token additions, and regeneration
86. via `document` or `init`. Never invoke these commands autonomously.
87. 
88. ### Impeccable lifecycle for code apps
89. 
90. | Phase | Command | When to use |
91. |-------|---------|-------------|
92. | **Before first app** | `document` | **Strongly recommended**: generates shared `code-apps/DESIGN.md` from existing code (or `new-work` if no code yet) |
93. | **Before each new app** | `init` | **Strongly recommended**: per-app PRODUCT.md — pins users, purpose, brand, constraints |
94. | **Before building** | `shape [feature]` | Plan UX/UI before writing code; runs a discovery interview and produces a design brief |
95. | **During development** | `hooks on` | Activates design detector — fires after every file edit and flags anti-patterns |
96. | **During development** | `live` | Interactive browser variant mode — pick elements, generate alternatives in real time |
97. | **Evaluate (pre-PR)** | `critique [target]` | UX review: visual hierarchy, IA, cognitive load, heuristic scoring |
98. | **Evaluate (pre-PR)** | `audit [target]` | Technical quality: a11y (WCAG), perf, responsive, anti-patterns (P0-P3 severity) |
99. | **Refine** | `polish [target]` | Final quality pass: alignment, spacing, consistency, micro-details |
100. | **Refine** | `harden [target]` | Production-ready: error states, i18n, text overflow, edge cases |
101. | **Refine** | `onboard [target]` | First-run flows, empty states, activation moments |
102. | **Targeted fix** | `adapt [target]` | Responsive and multi-device adaptation |
103. | **Targeted fix** | `layout [target]` | Spacing, rhythm, visual hierarchy |
104. | **Targeted fix** | `clarify [target]` | UX copy, labels, error messages |
105. | **Targeted fix** | `typeset [target]` | Typography hierarchy and font choices |
106. | **Targeted fix** | `optimize [target]` | UI performance: loading, rendering, bundle size |
107. | **Enhance** | `colorize / animate / delight` | Strategic color, motion, personality |
108. | **Maintenance** | `doctor` | Detects and repairs drift between PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md, and .impeccable/ artifacts |
109. 
110. **Mandatory gates for new apps:** `document` (if first app or no DESIGN.md) → `init` → `shape` → `hooks on`
111. 
112. **Pre-PR gates:** `critique` + `audit` before opening a pull request. Surface Critical/High findings to the user.
113. 
114. If the user explicitly skips `document` or `init`, proceed but record the gap and surface it at
115. review time. Never disable or silently ignore design hook findings.
116. 
117. If the `impeccable` skill is unavailable, flag the gap and do not attempt to reproduce its
118. behaviour manually.

121.

123. |-----------|-------------|
124. | `create-code-app` | Start any new app — always the first step |

136. ## Project conventions
137. 
138. ### App folder structure
139. All code apps live under `code-apps/<app-name>/` at the repo root.
140. Never create app files outside this path.
141. 
142. ### Preferred data source
143. Prefer Dataverse as the primary data source.
144. - New app with data needs → `add-dataverse` unless there is an explicit reason not to.
145. - Unclear source → `add-datasource` (it selects the best connector).
146. - Non-Dataverse sources are valid when the data lives there natively (SharePoint lists,
147.   Excel workbooks, etc.).
148. 
149. ### Generated files are read-only
150. Never edit files under `src/generated/` by hand.
151. These files are regenerated automatically when connector sub-skills run.
152. Hand edits will be overwritten and may corrupt the connector binding.
153. 
154. ### Pre-push quality gates (Makefile contract)
155. Use gate targets to keep terminology aligned across app and solution work:
156. 
157. - `app-gate` = `app-lint` + `app-test`
158. - `solution-gate` = `solution-pack` + `solution-check`

161. 1. `make app-gate` — mandatory for code-app changes.
162. 2. `make build` — optional confidence gate.
163. 3. `make solution-gate` — required when solution artifacts change.
164. 
165. If any required gate fails, fix errors before deploying.
166. 
167. ### Premium connector confirmation
168. Before adding any premium connector via `add-connector`:
169. 1. Identify the connector tier (premium vs. standard).
170. 2. Surface the DLP policy implications to the user.
171. 3. **Wait for explicit human confirmation** before executing `add-connector`.
172. 
173. This applies even in autopilot mode. Premium connectors affect licensing and DLP — the
174. human must acknowledge before the connector is added.
175.

181.        ├─ Missing dependency? → ask to install/enable → stop until resolved
182.        └─ Scope gate (environment + solution explicit)

186.                  └─ Yes (or approved) → impeccable init (per-app PRODUCT.md) → wait for human approval before writing

191.                                           └─ make app-gate
192.                                                └─ [optional] make build
193.                                                     └─ [if solution changed] make solution-gate
194.                                                          └─ deploy
195. ```
196. 
197. ```
198. Modify existing app
199.   └─ Dependency preflight
200.        ├─ Missing dependency? → ask to install/enable → stop until resolved
201.        └─ Scope gate (environment + solution explicit)
202.             ├─ Missing or ambiguous? → ask user → stop until resolved
203.             └─ Design context (impeccable context — if PRODUCT.md/DESIGN.md exist)

207.                       └─ No new source → edit, then make app-gate
208.                            └─ [optional] make build

213. ## Escape hatches

215. - If `create-code-app` fails due to environment targeting, run `route-environments` from
216.   the `power-automate` plugin to verify the active environment, then retry.
217. - If `deploy` fails with a DLP error, surface the full error message to the user and pause

219. - If the `impeccable` skill is unavailable, proceed without the design preflight but flag

221.   manually.

60. ## Project conventions

62. ### 1 — Solution-bound flows only
63. Every flow must be created inside a Dataverse solution.
64. Standalone flows (not inside a solution) are not committed to this repo.

95. 1. Present the flow name, solution, trigger, and estimated run frequency.
96. 2. **Wait for explicit human approval.**

118.        ├─ Missing dependency? → ask to install/enable → stop until resolved
119.        └─ Scope gate (environment + solution explicit)
120.             ├─ Missing or ambiguous? → ask user → stop until resolved

13. # data-management
14. 
15. Orchestration layer for all Dataverse operations in this project.
16. Always load `dv-overview` first — it provides cross-cutting safety rules, the tool-capability
17. map, and the safe-change lifecycle that every other sub-skill depends on.
18. 
19. ## Step 0 — Dependency preflight (required)
20. 
21. Before routing any task, verify the `dataverse` plugin sub-skills are available:
22. `dv-overview`, `dv-connect`, `dv-query`, `dv-data`, `dv-metadata`, `dv-solution`,
23. `dv-admin`, and `dv-security`.
24. 
25. If any required sub-skill is missing or unavailable:
26. 1. Stop execution and return a blocked status.
27. 2. Ask the user whether they want to install or enable the missing dependency.
28. 3. Resume only after availability is confirmed.
29. 
30. Do not attempt Dataverse work through ad-hoc fallback logic when these dependencies are missing.
31. 
32. ## Step 1 — Environment and solution scope gate (required)
33. 
34. Before any Dataverse work starts, the target scope must be explicit:
35. - Environment: display name and environment ID (or URL)
36. - Solution: unique name and publisher prefix
37. 
38. If either environment or solution is missing, ambiguous, or inferred:
39. 1. Stop execution and return a blocked status.
40. 2. Ask the user to explicitly provide the target environment and solution.
41. 3. Resume only after both are confirmed.
42. 
43. Do not proceed using defaults, recent-session guesses, or partial scope values.
44. 
45. ## Sub-skill routing
46. 
47. | Task | Sub-skill |
48. |------|-----------|
49. | First step of any Dataverse session | `dv-overview` |
50. | Connection missing, auth broken, MCP not responding | `dv-connect` |
51. | Read, filter, paginate, aggregate records | `dv-query` |
52. | Create / update / delete records; CSV import; bulk ops; seed data | `dv-data` |
53. | Author tables, columns, relationships, forms, views | `dv-metadata` |
54. | Create, export, import, promote solutions across environments | `dv-solution` |
55. | Bulk delete, retention/archival, org settings, recycle bin, audit | `dv-admin` |
56. | Security roles, users, business units, app user registration | `dv-security` |
57. 
58. Read `references/sub-skill-detail.md` when you need parameter-level guidance for a specific
59. sub-skill call.
60. 
61. ## Project conventions (mandatory)
62. 
63. ### 1 — Solution-first schema changes
64. All schema changes (new tables, columns, relationships, forms, views) **must** be encapsulated
65. inside a Dataverse solution before they are applied to any environment.
66. Never apply raw, unpackaged schema changes directly to an environment.
67. 
68. Before creating any table or column, call `dv-metadata` with a check-first instruction:
69. query whether a managed solution already defines that component in the target environment.
70. If it does, work with the existing component rather than creating a duplicate.
71. 
72. ### 2 — Sequencing for mixed tasks
73. When a task spans schema changes **and** data operations **and** solution lifecycle:
74. 
75. ```
76. 1. Schema changes via dv-metadata
77. 2. Validate (run dv-overview safe-change checklist)
78. 3. Pack / export solution via dv-solution
79. 4. Data operations via dv-data
80. ```
81. 
82. Never run data operations against schema that has not yet been promoted into a solution.
83. 
84. ### 3 — Destructive operations require human confirmation
85. `dv-admin` bulk-delete and archival operations **must** receive explicit human confirmation
86. before execution. Present the scope (table, filter, estimated row count) and wait for approval.
87. Do not self-approve bulk deletes even when operating in autopilot mode.
88. 
89. ### 5 — Artifact persistence for data and schema operations
90. 
91. Every artifact generated during a session that **modifies data or the data model** must be
92. saved to the `data/` directory at the repo root before execution. This includes:
93. - FetchXML / OData queries used to write, update, or delete records
94. - CSV files for bulk import
95. - Schema definition scripts (column, table, or relationship specs passed to `dv-metadata`)
96. - Bulk-delete filters passed to `dv-admin`
97. 
98. Read-only queries (exploration, filtering, reporting) do not require persistence unless the
99. user explicitly requests it.
100. 
101. **Naming convention:** `YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_<short-description>.<ext>`
102. 
103. Examples:
104. - `20260731_142055_add-account-industry-column.json`
105. - `20260731_151230_bulk-import-contacts.csv`
106. - `20260731_163400_delete-orphan-activity-records.fetchxml`
107. 
108. The Dataverse sub-skills generate and execute their own artifacts autonomously — typically
109. Python scripts using the official Dataverse Python SDK (`PowerPlatform-Dataverse-Client`),
110. CSV files, or other payloads. The orchestrator must not pre-write these artifacts.
111. 
112. After the sub-skill generates an artifact, **save or copy it to `data/`** using the naming
113. convention above. If the operation succeeded, leave the file as-is. If it failed, append
114. `_FAILED` to the filename so the failure is traceable without ambiguity.
115. 
116. ### 4 — Environment targeting
117. 
118. Always confirm the target environment before any write operation. Use `dv-connect` to verify
119. the active connection. Surface the environment display name and URL in your response so the
120. human can catch mis-targeting before changes land.
121. 
122. ## Decision tree
123. 
124. ```
125. Dataverse task received
126.   └─ Dependency preflight
127.        ├─ Missing dependency? → ask to install/enable → stop until resolved
128.        └─ Scope gate (environment + solution explicit)
129.             ├─ Missing or ambiguous? → ask user → stop until resolved
130.             └─ Load dv-overview (always)
131.                  ├─ Connection broken? → dv-connect, then retry
132.                  ├─ Read-only query? → dv-query
133.                  ├─ Record write (CRUD / import)?
134.                  │    ├─ Schema missing? → dv-metadata first (see §2 sequencing)
135.                  │    └─ dv-data → save generated artifact to data/ (YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_desc.ext)
136.                  ├─ Schema authoring?
137.                  │    └─ Check managed solutions → dv-metadata → save generated artifact to data/
138.                  ├─ Solution lifecycle? → dv-solution
139.                  ├─ Security / roles? → dv-security
140.                  └─ Bulk delete / org settings?
141.                       └─ confirm human → dv-admin → save generated artifact to data/
142. ```
143. 
144. ## Escape hatches
145. 
146. - If `dv-metadata` and `dv-solution` are both needed in a single session, keep a running
147.   checklist of components added so the solution export includes all of them.
148. - If the environment has no Dataverse instance, `dv-overview` will surface a warning — stop
149.   and report to the user rather than continuing with PPAPI-only fallback for schema work.

17. # solution-management
18. 
19. Orchestration layer for Power Platform solution lifecycle in the Dev environment.

22. deploy solutions to higher environments; that boundary is owned by the GitHub workflow.

24. ## Step 0 — Dependency preflight (required)
25. 
26. Before any solution work, verify the primary sub-skill is available:
27. - `dv-solution` from the `dataverse` plugin (microsoft/Dataverse-skills)
28. 
29. If `dv-solution` is unavailable, check for `pac` CLI as fallback:
30. - Run `pac --version` to confirm availability.

32. If neither is available:
33. 1. Stop execution and return a blocked status.
34. 2. Ask the user whether they want to install or enable the missing dependency.
35. 3. Resume only after at least one option is confirmed.
36. 
37. Tool priority for all operations in this skill:
38. 1. `dv-solution` sub-skill (preferred — higher-level, safer, plugin-managed)
39. 2. `pac` CLI (fallback — when `dv-solution` does not cover the operation)
40. 3. Raw Power Platform API / `az` CLI (last resort only — flag explicitly before using)
41. 
42. ## Step 1 — Environment and solution scope gate (required)
43. 
44. Before any solution work starts, require explicit target scope:
45. - Environment: Dev environment display name and environment ID (or URL)
46. - Solution: unique name and publisher prefix

48. If either is missing, ambiguous, or inferred:
49. 1. Stop execution and return a blocked status.

51. 3. Resume only after both are confirmed.

54. targeting staging or production must be rejected — point the user to the GitHub workflow.
55. 
56. ## Operations and tool routing
57. 
58. ### Solution creation
59. 
60. Goal: ensure the solution exists in the Dev environment with the correct publisher and prefix.
61. 
62. 1. Use `dv-solution` to check whether the solution already exists.
63. 2. If it does not exist, use `dv-solution` to create it (publisher + prefix required).
64. 3. If `dv-solution` cannot create directly, fall back to `pac solution create` CLI.
65. 
66. ### Local clone and sync
67. 
68. Goal: keep local solution files current with the Dev environment state.
69. 
70. - First clone: `dv-solution` export + unpack, or `pac solution clone` as fallback.
71. - Subsequent sync: `dv-solution` pull / sync operation, or `pac solution sync` as fallback.
72. - Solution files live under `solutions/<solution-unique-name>/` at the repo root.
73. - Never manually edit files under `solutions/<solution-unique-name>/Other/` — they are
74.   managed by the tooling.

78. Goal: produce `solutions/<solution-unique-name>/deployment-settings.json` containing all
79. connection references and environment variable definitions, with placeholder values for
80. non-Dev environments.
81. 
82. 1. `dv-solution` — use if it exposes a settings-generation operation.
83. 2. `pac solution generate-settings` — primary fallback (CLI).
84. 3. Manual inspection of the unpacked solution XML — last resort; flag to user.
85. 
86. After generation, verify every connection reference and environment variable in the solution
87. has a corresponding entry. Surface any gaps to the user before proceeding.
88. 
89. ### Solution checker
90. 
91. Goal: validate the solution against Power Platform best-practice rules before a PR.
92. 
93. 1. `dv-solution` — use if it exposes a checker operation.
94. 2. `pac solution check` — primary fallback (CLI).
95. 
96. Always run with the standard ruleset. Surface all Critical and High severity findings to
97. the user and block the PR recommendation until they are addressed or explicitly waived.

99. ### Solution pack (pre-PR artifact)
100. 
101. Goal: produce a clean `.zip` pack of the local solution for CI consumption.
102. 
103. 1. `dv-solution` — use if it exposes a pack operation.
104. 2. `pac solution pack` — primary fallback (CLI).
105. 
106. Pack is the last step before opening a PR. Never pack a solution that has failing checker
107. results (Critical/High) unless the user has explicitly waived them.
108. 
109. ### Dependency hygiene
110. 
111. Goal: identify and flag dependency risks in the solution before changes are committed.
112. 
113. Check for:
114. - Components that depend on managed solutions not listed as explicit dependencies
115. - Circular or implicit dependencies between solutions in the same publisher
116. - Unmanaged customisations layered on top of managed components
117. 
118. Use `dv-solution` introspection first; fall back to inspecting the unpacked solution XML.
119. Surface findings as warnings — do not auto-fix dependency issues without human guidance.
120. 
121. ## Standard workflows
122. 
123. ```
124. Start of a feature session
125.   └─ Step 0: dependency preflight
126.        └─ Step 1: scope gate (Dev env + solution explicit)
127.             ├─ Solution missing in Dev? → create (dv-solution → pac fallback)
128.             └─ Solution exists
129.                  ├─ Not cloned locally? → clone (dv-solution → pac fallback)
130.                  └─ Already cloned? → sync (dv-solution → pac fallback)
131.                       └─ deployment-settings.json current? → generate if not
132.                            └─ Hand off to content skills (data / agent / app / flow)
133. ```
134. 
135. ```
136. Pre-PR quality gate
137.   └─ Sync (pull latest Dev state)
138.        └─ deployment-settings.json up to date? → regenerate if not
139.             └─ solution checker (dv-solution → pac fallback)
140.                  ├─ Critical/High findings? → block → surface to user
141.                  └─ Clean (or waived) → pac solution pack
142.                       └─ Ready for PR
143. ```
144. 
145. ## Hard boundaries
146. 
147. | Action | Status | Reason |
148. |--------|--------|--------|
149. | `pac solution import` / `dv-solution` import to staging/prod | **Forbidden** | Deployment is the GitHub workflow |
150. | Write operations targeting non-Dev environments | **Forbidden** | Dev only for agent-driven work |
151. | Auto-fixing dependency issues | **Blocked** | Requires human guidance |
152. | Packing with unresolved Critical/High checker findings | **Blocked** | Unless user explicitly waives |
153. 
154. ## Escape hatches

156. - If `dv-solution` and `pac` both fail for an operation, surface the raw error + the
157.   manual XML-based fallback steps rather than attempting a raw API call silently.
158. - If the solution has multiple layers (managed base + unmanaged top), document which layer
159.   is being operated on before any export or pack.
160. - If `deployment-settings.json` already exists and is more recent than the last sync,
161.   ask the user whether to overwrite or merge before regenerating.
